title: Packing for the March
premise: Play a young person of the settlement in the last two days before the garrison leaves Fort Dearborn, 13 and 14 August 1812: choose your errands, and pack for the march.

opening.text:
JAUNT: PACKING FOR THE MARCH. August 1812, and you are twelve years old. Your household lives in a log house outside the pickets of Fort Dearborn, on the south bank of the Chicago River. The United States is at war with Britain, and the general at Detroit has ordered the fort given up. In two days the garrison walks out, and your household walks with it.

The places and the records are real; the young person is you. You will not meet the captain or the chief, and nobody will tell you everything. Watch, carry, and choose your errands.

stops.text: Thursday, 13 August 1812, morning, on the north bank. Across the river stands the fort, and on this side 'the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' On the 9th, Heald wrote, the general's order came: give up the post. 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' advice was to stay and fortify. Captain Heald will obey. At nine on the 15th the garrison marches for Detroit, with the women and children and the twelve men of the town's militia. Your household lives outside the pickets, and everything it owns must be sorted: what is carried, what is given away, what is left. Your mother has two errands for you across the river.
stops.narrative: Which errand first: the factory, or the gate?

choices.label: To the factory, where the goods are going out
choices.consequence: You will see what the garrison gives away.

choices.label: To the gate, to listen for news
choices.consequence: You will hear who is coming in before anyone tells you.

stops.text: Afternoon at the factory, the government's trading house, a log house just south-west of the fort. The goods are going out: 'blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints'. Heald's own report says he gave 'all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' General Hull's order allowed it, naming 'the Friendly Indians' who might escort the garrison to Fort Wayne. It also named 'the Poor & needy of your Post.' Your household is poor enough to be counted. Next door is the agent's house, its piazzas 'planked up, for greater security', with port-holes cut. You carry home a bolt of calico, and nothing else.
stops.narrative: What the garrison cannot carry, it gives away.

stops.text: Afternoon at the main gate, in the middle of the south side. The fort is a square of barracks with two blockhouses at opposite corners, 'inclosed within a double row of palisades'. Riders come in: Captain William Wells of Fort Wayne, Heald's report says, 'with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in'. Wau-Bun puts him here a day later, and says he came 'all too late'. Wells is the uncle of Rebekah Heald, the captain's wife. Nobody at the gate stops to explain any of this to you. You listen, and carry the news home with the water bucket.
stops.narrative: News comes in at the gate before it reaches anyone's house.

stops.text: Evening, on the river side of the fort's north-east corner. A covered way runs from here down to the water. Tonight the soldiers are busy in it. 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well'. The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well' too. The rest of the liquor goes out of the northern gate, 'the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' Heald feared 'they would make bad use of it'. It is meant to be secret, but the knocking carries, and next morning the water tastes of 'strong grog'. Your household's water comes from this river.
stops.narrative: Draw water upstream tonight, or wait until morning?

choices.label: Fill the keg upstream tonight
choices.consequence: Your household will have clean water for the walk.

choices.label: Stay near the fort tomorrow
choices.consequence: You will see who comes and goes on the last day.

stops.text: Friday, 14 August, morning, where the river meets the lake, half a mile below the fort. Across the water Captain Whistler once drew 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River', and wrote that the fort was 'perfectly secure from any ambuscade'. Wau-Bun says Mrs. Kinzie's boat will come down to this river mouth tomorrow, while the column walks. Your keg is full and stoppered, and today you sort the rest: a blanket each, the pot, the calico or the news, and the things that stay behind. Tomorrow the column takes the beach south, 'with the lake on our left'.
stops.narrative: The last full day, spent packing.

stops.text: Friday, 14 August, evening, on the parade inside the fort, beside the commanding officer's quarters. Black Partridge, 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River', has come in. Wau-Bun says he 'entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his peace medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Lieutenant Helm and Sergeant Griffith both recorded his warning. You see no more than a door closing across the parade, and you hear about the medal afterwards, as everyone does. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens.
stops.narrative: A warning on the last evening.

legs.note: Across the river by canoe, then south past the fort to the factory.
legs.story: The river first, then the long side of the pickets.

legs.note: Across the river by canoe, then round the pickets to the main gate on the south.
legs.story: Round to the gate where the news comes in.

legs.note: North round the pickets to the river side of the fort.
Round the east side of the pickets to the river corner.
Down the bank to the river mouth, half a mile below the fort.
In at the gate to the parade.

endings.text: Night on the 14th. The bundle is tied: the calico folded under the blankets, the keg stoppered beside the pot. You did both errands and kept the water clean. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens and the column walks south along the beach. What happened there that morning is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. You carried home the news from the gate, and tonight you carry home the story of the medal. Everyone in the settlement is telling it. Nobody can unpack now: tomorrow at nine the gate opens and the column walks south along the beach. What happened there that morning is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. The calico from the factory is folded on top of the bundle, and you watched the last evening at the fort. You know now how much was given away, and why. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens. What happened on the beach that morning is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

Night on the 14th. The keg is full, the bundle is tied, and you know who rode in at the gate. Tomorrow at nine the gate opens and the column walks south. What happened on the beach that morning is told in the jaunt The Battle of Fort Dearborn.

keepsake.title: A Bundle for the March
keepsake.text: A fictional list of what one household outside the pickets packed for the march of 15 August 1812. No real household, bundle or child is recorded on it.

evidence.text: Heald's journal: 'On the 9th of Augt, 1812, rec'd orders from Genl Wm. Hull to evacuate the Post of Chicago and proceed with my Command to Detroit.' Quaife: 'The next day the Indian runner. Winnemac, delivered to Captain Heald at Fort Dearborn his order for the evacuation.' Wau-Bun puts the runner, Winnemeg or Catfish, a Potawatomi, at the post on the 7th, bringing despatches that 'announced the declaration of war between the United States and Great Britain'. Wau-Bun: 'The order for evacuating the post was read next morning upon parade', and the officers' 'unanimous advice was, to remain where they were, and fortify themselves as strongly as possible.' Quaife defends Heald: 'Obedience to orders is the primary duty of a soldier.'
evidence.locator: Quaife Appendix III (Heald's journal) and the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun (1856): 'On the north side of the main stream, but quite near its junction with Lake Michigan, stood (as has already been described) the dwelling-house and trading-establishment of Mr. Kinzie.' 'The fort was situated on the southern bank, directly opposite this mansion'. The Chicago Reader (2018): in January 1812 Heald made 'Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth' the exclusive fort sutlers. Kirkland (1893): Margaret Helm was the 'step-daughter of old John Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: Wau-Bun, the April section; the Reader, the sutler paragraph; Kirkland, the Helm narrative

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 15th, at 9 o'clock in the morning, we commenced our march: a part of the Miamies were detached in front, and the remainder in our rear, as guards, under the direction of Captain Wells. The situation of the country rendered it necessary for us to take the beach, with the lake on our left, and a high sand bank on our right, at about 100 yards distance.' Wau-Bun: 'As the troops left the fort, the band struck up the Dead March', and Wells 'had blackened his face before leaving the garrison, in token of his impending fate.' Mrs. Kinzie's boat 'had scarcely reached the mouth of the river, which, it will be recollected, was here half a mile below the fort, when another messenger from To-pee-nee-bee arrived to detain them where they were.' Quaife lists the order: Wells and part of the Miamis, the garrison, the women and children, the twelve Chicago militia.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the battle chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XIX, Narrative of the Massacre, Continued, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 14th, I delivered the Indians all the goods in the factory store, and a considerable quantity of provisions which we could not take away with us.' Wau-Bun, which dates it the 13th: 'the goods, consisting of blankets, broadcloths, calicoes, paints, etc., were distributed, as stipulated.'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: General William Hull's order, Sandwich, 29 July 1812, found among the Heald papers and first printed by Quaife: 'It is with regret I order the Evacuation of your Post owing to the want of Provisions only a neglect of the Commandant' ... 'You will therefore Destroy all arms & ammunition, but the Goods of the Factory you may give to the Friendly Indians who may be desirous of Escorting you on to Fort Wayne & to the Poor & needy of your Post.'
evidence.locator: note 583, Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the evacuation chapter

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'A short distance to the southwest were two log houses, one occupied by Matthew Irwin, the United States factor, and the other by Charles Jouett, the Indian agent.' Wau-Bun (1856) on the Agency House in April 1812: 'It was an old-fashioned log building, with a hall running through the centre, and one large room on each side. Piazzas extended the whole length of the building in front and rear. These were planked up, for greater security, port-holes were cut, and sentinels posted at night.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text, the paragraph beginning 'It was an old-fashioned log building'

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'On the 13th, Captain Wells, of Fort Wayne, arrived with about 30 Miamies, for the purpose of escorting us in, by the request of General Hull.' Wau-Bun has him arrive on the 14th 'with fifteen friendly Miamis' to save 'his relative, Captain Heald', and says he came 'all too late': the ammunition was already destroyed. Quaife: Heald's wife Rebekah was 'the niece of Captain Wells'.
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Quaife (1913), from Cooper and Whistler's draught: 'The barracks and other structures for the accommodation of the garrison were built around the four sides of a quadrangle, facing inward toward the center. Two blockhouses, one containing two small cannon, the other containing one, stood at the northwestern and southeastern corners of the quadrangle, and the whole was inclosed within a double row of palisades'. 'Thus if an enemy should scale the first row he would only find himself within a narrow inclosure between that and the second which was swept at every point by the fire from the blockhouses.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure')

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): the barracks 'were two stories in height, with shingled roofs and covered galleries, and occupied the middle of each side of the inclosure facing toward the parade ground, in the center of which stood a lofty flagstaff. The commanding officer's quarters stood on the east side, and directly opposite were those for the subordinate officers. The main gateway of the stockade was at the middle of the south side and was flanked on either side by the main barracks for the common soldiers.' Whistler's own note: 'the Barracks are two storeys high with shingled Roofs and Galliaries fronting the parade.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text)

evidence.text: Heald's report: 'The surplus arms and ammunition I thought proper to destroy, fearing they would make bad use of it if put in their possession. I also destroyed all the liquor on hand after they began to collect.' Wau-Bun: 'The same evening the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency; the remainder was transported as secretly as possible through the northern gate, the heads of the barrels knocked in, and the contents poured into the river.' The muskets 'were broken up and thrown into the well'. The noise betrayed it, and 'the taste of the water the next morning was, as one expressed it, "strong grog."'
evidence.locator: Appendix IV, Captain Heald's official report, Pittsburg, 23 October 1812 (from Brannan, Official Military and Naval Letters, 1823, p. 84), Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text; Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'From the northeast corner of the stockade a covered way led to the river, securing thus to the garrison access in safety to the water in time of attack.' Whistler's index lists 'Covered Way to procure Water' and 'Gutters to carry off the Water' as 'Omited in their places'. Wau-Bun remembers 'a sally-port, or subterranean passage from the parade-ground to the river', and on 13 August 1812 'the ammunition and liquor were carried, part into the sally-port, and thrown into a well which had been dug there to supply the garrison with water in case of emergency'.
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, the description of the fort (Project Gutenberg eBook #69274 plain text, the paragraphs beginning 'There exist two contemporary pictures' and 'Within the stockaded inclosure'); Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text); Wau-Bun ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text

evidence.text: Wau-Bun: on the evening after the second council 'Black Partridge, a conspicuous chief, entered the quarters of the commanding officer' and gave back his medal: 'I will not wear a token of peace while I am compelled to act as an enemy.' Quaife: Black Partridge was 'a Pottawatomie chief from the Illinois River' (a Potawatomi leader); of the two contemporary versions, Lieutenant Helm's and Sergeant Griffith's through McAfee, both record his warning and 'Helm alone mentions the surrender of the medal.'
evidence.locator: ch. XVIII, Massacre at Chicago, Project Gutenberg eBook #12183 plain text; Quaife, the evacuation chapter and note 591

evidence.text: Wells reached the fort on the 13th by Heald's report or the 14th by Wau-Bun; Black Partridge came to the commanding officer 'on the evening' after the second council. This stop is set at sunset on 14 August, the eve of the march.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun's 'evening succeeding the council' and the march next morning; the hour is a reading of 'evening'.

evidence.text: Whistler, 20 February 1808, closing his note to the draught: 'At this time the Garrison (except the Houses on the Opisite side of the river being somewhat in the way) is perfectly secure from any ambuscade or Barrier.' His index numbers the 'Wharf of said River' and 'John Kinzie Esq. House on the opisite side River'. He had already had a picket fence across the river taken up, since it 'might serve as a Barrier against the Garrison', and 'replaced with a common rail fence.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, ch. VI, footnote 413, 'Index annexed to the draught of Fort Dearborn &c.', Whistler, 20 February 1808 (Gutenberg #69274 plain text), Whistler's note

evidence.text: The walk runs over the last two days before the march of 15 August 1812: the 13th, when Wau-Bun has the factory goods given out and, that evening, the ammunition and liquor sunk, and Heald's report has Wells come in; and the 14th, the evening Black Partridge gave back his medal. The hours of the stops are the jaunt's pacing; no source gives them.
evidence.reasoning: Wau-Bun dates the goods to the 13th and the well 'The same evening'; Heald's report dates the goods to the 14th and Wells to the 13th, and Wau-Bun has Wells on the 14th. The medal came on the evening after the second council, read as the 14th as The Battle of Fort Dearborn reads it. The hours are chosen to walk the two days in order, not recorded.

evidence.text: The six stops are scene anchors of 1812 that the published 1812 jaunts already use: the front of the Kinzie house on the north bank, the factory front, the main gate, the covered way at the north-east corner, the parade and the river mouth. No interior is entered and no doorway is claimed.
evidence.reasoning: The anchors and their positions are the ones The Battle of Fort Dearborn and Fort Dearborn, Building by Building stand on, read from Whistler's 1808 draught, Quaife's description of the fort and Wau-Bun's placing of the Kinzie house opposite it. This jaunt adds no place.

evidence.text: The young person the visitor plays, their age, their household outside the pickets and its packing, the errands, the order of the route, the two choices, the four endings, the timing inputs and the A Bundle for the March keepsake are invented connective narrative. No such young person is recorded or named, no named person is met or speaks to them, no known child of a named family is given a part, and nothing is staged at any stop.
